newsitem.title: USA: EEOC to monitor Texaco discrimination compliance.
newsitem.headline: EEOC to monitor Texaco discrimination compliance.

text.p: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission reached a five-year agreement with Texaco Inc. Friday to intervene in a racial discrimination case and monitor the company's promotion of minorities.
"I would say that the level of scrutiny that Texaco will have to undergo is substantially higher than is usual in these kinds of settlements," said James Lee, regional attorney for the EEOC.

Texaco agreed on Nov. 15 to pay $176.1 million to settle a lawsuit filed by black employees who alleged they were discriminated against in pay and promotions. The plaintiffs said it was the biggest settlement in a race discrimination case in the United States.
The settlement is still tentative and must be approved by a federal judge. The agreement between the EEOC and Texaco is contingent on that final approval.
U.S. District Judge Charles Brieant set a hearing for Feb. 27 to consider the settlement.
A Texaco spokesman said the company was satisfied with the agreement and said the EEOC's intervention was not seen as intrusive.

The commission sought to intervene in the lawsuit because it was troubled that it had been excluded from the settlement talks. It has been negotiating with Texaco for a role in monitoring the company's compliance with the settlement terms, which include plans to establish an "equality and tolerance" task force.
"Our concern was future compliance ... to ensure they have not bought their way out of trouble," Lee told reporters following a court hearing where the accord was announced.

Under the EEOC agreement presented to Brieant here, the commission can monitor Texaco's compliance with federal law that prohibits workplace discrimination by inspecting Texaco's premises and records and interviewing current or former salaried employees.
The pact provides that within a year of its effective date and annually for the next five years, Texaco must give the EEOC a report that gives information about vacancies filled by promotion.

For every vacancy filled, Texaco must describe the job opening, outside recruitment notices, internal job posting and documentation of career ladders. The company must also provide information about the qualifications of individual employees and compensation history.

As part of the settlement, White Plains, N.Y.-based Texaco released a plan last month to boost employment, career development and recruiting of minorities, as well as increasing purchasing from minority- and women-owned companies.
The plan was well-received by lawyers representing the black plaintiffs and the Rev. Jesse Jackson, who responded by calling for an end to a consumer boycott of Texaco he helped initiate in November.

Daniel Berger, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, told the judge the formal settlement agreement will be filed by next Friday. He said notices of the settlement will be mailed to other potential members of the class-action by Jan. 17 and that those who object or wish to opt out must notify the court by Feb. 20.

Problems at Texaco surfaced after plaintiffs' lawyers in the discrimination suit received secret tapes of senior executives discussing the destruction of damaging documents. The executives allegedly also made racist remarks.
